title: Change authority, the change budget and concessions
blurb: Explain who may approve changes, why delegated authority needs a change budget, and what a concession is.
question: The board has given a change authority power to approve small changes. A large request for change arrives. Who decides, how is the change paid for, and what happens if a product is accepted short of its specification?

teach.body: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications. It may delegate some of that authority, within limits, to a change authority (a person or group) or to the project manager. In plain English: the board keeps the final say, but it can let others decide smaller changes so that it is not swamped and decisions are made quickly at the right level.

head: Who
Authority over changes
rows: Ultimate authority; decides whether and to whom to delegate
Approves within the limits the board delegates
May be given delegated authority within limits
Implements approved changes in a work package
teach.caption: The arrangement is documented in the issue management approach and the role descriptions.

teach.body: Delegation is about approving changes, not implementing them: approved changes are still carried out through work packages under the project manager's control. The board decides whether to delegate and to whom, and the delegated authority should be reviewed at each stage boundary or whenever tolerances change. Anything beyond the delegated limits is escalated to the next level up.

teach.h: Who decides this request for change?

children.label: Escalate to the project board
children.sub: the board approves, rejects or asks for more

teach.body: The change budget is money, or a set of authorized constraints within which trade-offs can be made, set aside in a plan to cover changes. It is allocated by those with delegated authority. The project manager should make sure delegated authority comes with a suitable change budget, because approving a change is pointless if there is nothing to fund it. A change with a cost is funded from the change budget or from additional customer funding.

An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications. It must go through change control, and the decision is either to correct it or to accept it as it is. Accepting an off-specification without corrective action is a concession. Concessions granted in a stage are confirmed to the board when the project manager requests the next stage, and highlighted again when the project manager requests project closure.

steps.label: Decide
steps.sub: correct it, or grant a concession

steps.label: Report
steps.sub: when requesting the next stage or closure

teach.body: Brackenridge University is replacing its student records system. Executive Helen Marsh and the board delegate change authority to a group led by senior user Kwame Asante, who may approve changes up to £5,000 each within a £30,000 change budget per stage. A £3,000 report tweak is approved by the group. A £14,000 request to add a mobile app goes beyond the limit, so project manager Lucy Chen escalates it to the board. Later, the group grants a concession for a screen that loads slightly slower than specified.

teach.text: Classic traps: the change authority is NOT the ultimate authority; the board is, and the change authority acts only within delegated limits. Delegation covers approving changes, not implementing them. And the change budget funds approved changes, while the risk budget funds risk responses.

items: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications.
The board may delegate to a change authority or the project manager, within limits; review it at each stage boundary or when tolerances change.
Delegation is about approving changes, not implementing them.
Change budget: money or authorized constraints set aside to cover changes; it should accompany delegated authority.
Concession: an off-specification accepted without corrective action.

summary: You can now explain that the board is the ultimate authority for changes but may delegate approval, within limits, to a change authority or the project manager. You can also describe the change budget that funds approved changes and the concession that accepts an off-specification as it is.

A.q: The project board has delegated some change decisions to a change authority. Which statement is correct?
options: The board remains the ultimate authority for requests for change
The change authority becomes the ultimate authority for changes
The change authority takes over setting the stage tolerances
The project manager becomes accountable for the business case
A.why: The board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications; a change authority approves within the limits the board delegates (manual 10.2.4).

whyNot.1: Delegation is within limits; ultimate authority stays with the board.
whyNot.2: Stage tolerances are set by the project board, not the change authority.
whyNot.3: The executive owns the business case; delegating change authority does not move that accountability.

options: Money set aside in a plan to fund agreed risk responses
An agreed range of permitted cost variation for a stage
Money or authorized constraints set aside to cover changes
A reserve held by the business layer to fund exceptions
A.why: The change budget is the money or authorized constraints set aside in a plan to cover changes, allocated by those with delegated authority.

whyNot.1: That is cost tolerance, a limit of delegated authority rather than a fund for changes.
whyNot.3: Exceptions are handled through exception reports and plans, not a change budget held by the business layer.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. An off-specification that is accepted without corrective action is known as a [?].
options: deferral
concession
change
dispensation
A.why: A concession is an off-specification that is accepted without corrective action.

whyNot.0: Deferring postpones a decision; it does not accept the product as it is.
whyNot.2: A change is a modification to an approved product in the baseline.
whyNot.3: Dispensation is not the PRINCE2 term; the method calls this a concession.

B.q:
Which two statements about delegated change authority are correct?
1. The change budget funds responses to identified risks.
2. Delegated change authority covers approving changes, not implementing them.
3. A change authority may approve changes above its limits when the matter is urgent.
4. Delegated change authority should be reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Delegation is about approving, not implementing (2), and it is reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change (4).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: risk responses are funded from the risk budget.
whyNot.1: Both are false: the change budget funds approved changes, and decisions beyond delegated limits are escalated.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is false: anything beyond the delegated limits is escalated, whatever its urgency.

B.q: Why should delegated change authority be accompanied by a change budget?
options: So the risk owner can fund responses to new threats
So approved changes can be funded and implemented
So the board no longer needs to set stage tolerances
So off-specifications can be closed without assessment
B.why: The project manager should ensure delegated authority comes with a change budget from which approved changes can be delivered (manual 10.2.5).

whyNot.0: Risk responses are funded from the risk budget.
whyNot.2: The board still sets stage tolerances; a change budget does not replace them.
whyNot.3: Off-specifications are assessed through change control before any decision.

B.q: Which pairing correctly shows what each budget funds?
options: Risk budget: approved changes; change budget: risk responses
Risk budget: exceptions; change budget: tolerance overruns
Risk budget: benefits reviews; change budget: concessions
Risk budget: risk responses; change budget: approved changes
B.why: The risk budget funds risk responses, and the change budget funds approved changes.

whyNot.1: Neither budget exists to fund exceptions or tolerance overruns; those go to the board through exception reports.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach, and a concession accepts a product without spending on correction.

C.q: A change authority may approve changes costing up to £5,000 each from its change budget. A request for change, assessed at £12,000, arrives. Who should decide it?
options: The change authority, as it holds the change budget
The project board, after the request is escalated
The project manager, as corrective action in the stage
The team manager, as part of the work package
C.why: The request is beyond the change authority's delegated limits, so it is escalated to the project board, the ultimate authority for changes.

whyNot.0: Holding the budget does not extend the limit; £12,000 is beyond the delegated authority.
whyNot.2: Corrective action keeps a stage within tolerance; approving a change to the baseline beyond delegated limits is for the board.
whyNot.3: Team managers implement approved changes; they do not approve them.

C.q: A delivered product misses one quality specification. The change authority agrees to accept it as it is. What is this decision, and when is it raised with the board?
options: A concession; when the next stage is requested
A deferral; in the next checkpoint report
A request for change; in an exception report
A concession; in the updated project brief
C.why: Accepting an off-specification without corrective action is a concession, and concessions in the stage are raised with the board when the project manager requests the next stage.

whyNot.1: The product has been accepted, not deferred, and checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager.
whyNot.2: Nobody is proposing a change, and no tolerance breach is forecast, so no exception report is needed.
whyNot.3: The project brief is a pre-project product from starting up a project; it is not where concessions are reported.

C.q: Which statement about delegating change authority is correct?
options: The team manager decides how much authority to delegate
The business layer appoints the change authority each stage
The project manager holds it by default for every change
The board decides whether to delegate it, and to whom
C.why: The project board decides whether to delegate change authority and to whom, documented in the issue management approach and role descriptions.

whyNot.0: Team managers implement changes; they do not decide on delegating authority.
whyNot.1: The board, not the business layer, delegates change authority for the project.
whyNot.2: The PM has change authority only if the board delegates it, within limits.

reteach.title: The office refurbishment
reteach.question: How does a facilities director keep control of a refurbishment without approving every small change herself?

blocks.body: The director tells her office manager: 'You can approve changes up to £500 each, from a £4,000 pot. Anything bigger comes to me.' A different paint colour is approved on the spot. A whole new kitchen comes to the director. When the carpet arrives a shade darker than ordered and the team decide to keep it, that is a concession: accepting what fell short instead of fixing it.

blocks.text: Permission to approve is useless without money to pay. That is why delegated change authority comes with a change budget.

explain.body: The board may delegate authority for approving requests for change and off-specifications to a change authority or to the project manager.

test.q: According to PRINCE2 7, to whom may the project board delegate authority to approve requests for change?
options: A team manager or project support
Project assurance or quality assurance
A change authority or the project manager
The business layer or a supplier company
test.why: The board may delegate authority for approving changes to a change authority or to the project manager (manual 10.2.4).

whyNot.0: Team managers implement approved changes and project support administers the issue register; the method does not name them as the delegates.
whyNot.1: Project assurance advises the board and quality assurance sits outside the project; the method does not name them as the delegates.
whyNot.3: The business layer sits above the board, so the board cannot delegate to it, and a supplier company is not a named delegate.

explain.body: Delegated change authority lets the delegate approve changes within limits. Building the changed products still happens through work packages.

test.q: What does delegated change authority give the delegate?
options: Authority to approve changes within limits
Responsibility for building changed products
Accountability for the project business case
Control over the project-level tolerances
test.why: Delegation is about approving changes within limits, not implementing them (manual 10.2.4).

whyNot.1: Building products is done by teams through work packages.
whyNot.2: The executive is accountable for the business case.
whyNot.3: Project tolerances are set by the business layer.

explain.body: A change budget is usually money earmarked for changes, but it can also be a set of authorized constraints within which trade-offs can be made.

test.q: Besides money, how else can a change budget be defined?
options: As a percentage of the risk budget for each stage
As an agreed overrun on the stage cost tolerance
As a share of the benefits the project will deliver
As a set of authorized constraints for trade-offs
test.why: A change budget can be defined as a set of authorized constraints within which trade-offs can be made (manual 10.2.5).

whyNot.0: The risk budget is separate and funds risk responses.
whyNot.1: Tolerance is a limit of delegated authority, not a change budget.
whyNot.2: Benefits are what the project aims to achieve, not a budget for changes.

explain.body: Once assessed, an off-specification is either corrected or accepted as it is. Accepting it without corrective action is a concession.

test.q: An off-specification has been assessed. Which pair of decisions is typical for it?
options: Transfer it to a third party, or accept it as a risk
Grant a concession, or reject it so it is corrected
Close it in the daily log, or move it to the lessons log
Ask for a new project brief, or close the project early
test.why: For an off-specification, the decision is typically to grant a concession or to reject it so it is put right.

whyNot.0: Transfer and accept are risk responses, not decisions on an off-specification.
whyNot.2: An off-specification goes through change control; it is not simply closed or turned into a lesson.
whyNot.3: A project brief is a pre-project product, and premature closure is a board decision for far bigger reasons.
